title: Design search autocomplete
summary: Suggestions on every keystroke within a few tens of milliseconds: a trie with the top-k stored at each node, an offline aggregation pipeline, CDN caching of popular prefixes and client debounce.

steps.title: Requirements and estimates
body: **The ask:** as the user types into the search box, show the 5 most popular completions of what they have
typed so far.
| Kind | Requirement |
| Functional | top 5 suggestions for a prefix; per language or region; trending queries show up within an hour or so |
| Non-functional | it must feel instant: under ~100 ms end to end, so a server budget of ~10-20 ms; very high availability (a broken box breaks search) |
| Out of scope | personalised suggestions, spelling correction (mention them as extensions) |
```text
users       50 M daily active, 6 searches each
requests    ~4 per search after debounce (not 1 per keystroke)
50 M x 6 x 4 = 1.2 B / day  ≈ 14,000 / s average, ~40,000 / s peak
data        top 10 M distinct queries x ~30 bytes ≈ 300 MB of strings; with the trie and top-k lists a few GB
It fits in **memory on every server**. So the design is about keeping lookups O(prefix length) and keeping the
data fresh, not about storage.

steps.prompt: How many suggestion requests per second on average? (Integer division.)
steps.explain: 1.2 B a day over 86,400 seconds. Without debouncing, a 12-character query would be 12 requests and the load three times higher.

steps.title: A trie with the answers already in it
body: ```text
(root)  top: weather, web mail, wedding
w     top: weather, web mail, wedding
e     top: weather, web mail, wedding
a    b    d ...
top: weather  top: web mail    top: wedding
Walking a trie to the prefix node is O(length of the prefix). If you then had to search the whole subtree for
the most popular completions, "w" would scan millions of queries. So each node **stores its top k** (say 5)
completions. A lookup is: walk the prefix, return the list. No search at request time.
The cost moves to **build time**: every node's list must be computed. That is why the trie is built **offline**:
```text
search logs --> hourly / daily aggregation (query, count, decayed by age) --> build trie snapshot
--> ship to every serving node --> load beside the old one --> switch atomically

steps.prompt: Why store the top-k completions at every node instead of computing them at request time?
options: A lookup then costs only the prefix length; computing at request time would walk huge subtrees for short prefixes like "w"
It uses less memory than storing the queries once
It makes the trie easier to update in real time
Tries cannot be searched without it
steps.explain: It is a classic trade: more memory (k strings or pointers per node) and a slower build, for predictable, tiny lookups on the hot path. Short prefixes are both the most common requests and the biggest subtrees.

steps.title: Caching, freshness and the client
body: - **CDN caching.** Suggestions for a prefix are the same for everyone in a region and language, so
`GET /suggest?q=wea&lang=en` is cacheable at the edge for a few minutes. The short prefixes, which are most of
the traffic, then never reach your servers.
- **Client debounce.** Send a request only after the user pauses typing for ~100-200 ms, cancel stale requests,
and cache answers in the page (backspace is free).
- **Freshness.** A daily batch misses breaking news. Add a small **real-time layer**: count the last hour's
queries in a stream processor and merge a few trending ones into the batch results.
- **Filtering.** Remove offensive or unsafe suggestions at build time, with a block list that can also be applied
instantly at serving time for emergencies.
- **Sharding**, if one server is not enough, by hash of the prefix's first characters, or simply replicate the
whole trie everywhere (it is a few GB).

steps.prompt: Does this happen offline (in the build pipeline) or online (on each request)?
items: Count queries from yesterday's search logs
Build a trie snapshot with the top-k at every node
Ship the snapshot to every serving node
Walk to the prefix node and return its stored list
Serve the cached answer for "wea" from the CDN

prompt: **Symptom first.** A major storm hits at 09:00. By 15:00 users still see no suggestion for "storm" when they type
"sto", although it is the top query of the day. The pipeline's job log:
trie-build   schedule: daily 02:00 UTC   last run: 02:00 UTC   ok   10.2 M queries
options: Add a real-time layer that counts recent queries (last hour, from a stream) and merges trending ones into the batch results
Run the full trie build every minute
Disable the CDN cache for suggestions
steps.explain: The daily build is fine for stable popularity; it simply cannot see today. A full rebuild every minute is expensive and slow to ship. A small streaming counter for recent queries is the usual answer, with the batch as the stable base.

steps.prompt: Match each technique to what it buys you.
pairs: Lookup cost depends only on the prefix length
A request only after the user pauses typing
Popular short prefixes answered at the edge
Serving nodes switch to a new trie atomically
Today's trending queries appear within the hour

steps.title: A trie with top-k suggestions
prompt: - `void Add(string query, long count)`: adds `count` to the query's total (it may be added more than once).
- `List<string> Suggest(string prefix)`: up to `k` queries that start with `prefix`, highest total first; equal
totals in ordinal string order. An unknown prefix gives an empty list; `""` matches every query.
Store the top-k list at each trie node and update it in `Add`, so `Suggest` only walks the prefix. Counts only
grow, so when a query's total rises it is enough to (re)insert **that** query into each node's list on its
path, re-sort and trim to `k`. Anything trimmed can only come back by being added again.
starter: public void Add(string query, long count) { }
solution: public readonly Dictionary<char, Node> Next = new();
public void Add(string query, long count)
if (!node.Next.TryGetValue(c, out var child)) node.Next[c] = child = new Node();
node.Top.Sort((a, b) => totals[a] != totals[b] ? totals[b].CompareTo(totals[a]) : string.CompareOrdinal(a, b));
if (!node.Next.TryGetValue(c, out var child)) return new List<string>();
hints: A node is a `Dictionary<char, Node>` of children plus a `List<string>` top list; keep the totals in one `Dictionary<string, long>`.
In `Add`, call an `Update(node, query)` on the root and on every node along the query: add it if missing, sort by total descending then `string.CompareOrdinal`, trim to `k`.
template: Dojo.Eq("top 3 for we", new List<string> { "weather", "web mail", "wedding" }, dojoA.Suggest("we"));
Dojo.Eq("a longer prefix narrows it", new List<string> { "weekend" }, dojoA.Suggest("wee"));
Dojo.Eq("counts add up and can climb into the top", new List<string> { "weekend", "weather", "web mail" }, dojoA.Suggest("we"));
Dojo.Eq("ties are broken in ordinal order", new List<string> { "weekend", "weather", "web mail" }, dojoA.Suggest("we"));
Dojo.Eq("the exact query is its own prefix", new List<string> { "wex" }, dojoA.Suggest("wex"));
Dojo.Eq("the empty prefix matches everything", new List<string> { "weekend", "weather", "web mail" }, dojoA.Suggest(""));
Dojo.Eq("an unknown prefix", new List<string>(), dojoA.Suggest("x"));
